messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Phan arrived at the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, a full twenty minutes early, having taken three separate buses to avoid the highway. He was seventy-two years old, a married man who had spent the better part of four decades working as a refugee aid worker for an international humanitarian organization. His hands, folded neatly on his lap, trembled slightly as he explained why he had come. He spoke in a low, careful voice, as if afraid that raising it might trigger something he could not control.

The event that had shattered his sense of safety occurred three years ago, during a field mission in a conflict zone. Phan had been coordinating the distribution of food supplies in a camp when a suicide bomber detonated a vest in the crowd. The blast wave threw him against a concrete wall. He remembered the sound first—a deafening, percussive roar that seemed to come from inside his own skull—and then the silence that followed, broken by screams and the wet, sucking sound of people trying to breathe. He had been knocked unconscious for several minutes. When he came to, he was lying on his back, staring at a sky filled with smoke and dust. He could hear a child crying somewhere to his left, and the distinct, rhythmic thud of helicopter blades growing louder. He tried to stand but his legs would not obey. For a long moment, he was certain he was dead, and that what he was seeing was not real. That feeling—the conviction that the memory could not possibly belong to his own life—had never entirely left him.

In the weeks that followed, Phan returned home to his wife in a quiet suburban town. He told himself he was fine. He went back to work remotely, answering emails from a home office. But the world had changed. The memory did not come as a coherent story; it came in flashes, mostly visual—the image of a shredded blue tarp flapping in the wind, a single sandal lying in the dirt—and sometimes sounds, the specific pitch of that child’s cry, the helicopter’s rotor thrum. He would be sitting at his desk and suddenly hear the blast in his head, so vivid that he would flinch and drop whatever he was holding. He began to startle at ordinary noises: a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the kettle whistling. His wife learned to announce herself before entering a room.

Phan’s mind, left to its own devices, turned against him. He found himself replaying the moment of the explosion, over and over, searching for what he could have done differently. He had been standing near the distribution point. He had seen a man in a heavy coat, even though it was hot. He had not said anything. He had not moved. He was certain, with a conviction that felt unshakable, that he should have seen it coming. He blamed himself for not acting, for not warning anyone, for surviving when others did not. This self-blame became a loop he could not exit, a private torture that occupied hours of his day.

He stopped driving. The act of sitting in a car, whether as driver or passenger, made his chest tighten and his breath grow shallow. He could not explain why, except that it felt like being trapped, like waiting for something to happen. He began to avoid any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. He stopped answering phone calls from colleagues, stopped attending virtual meetings where there might be debate. He told his wife he was tired. He told himself he was protecting his peace. In truth, he had come to believe that any conflict, no matter how minor, could escalate into catastrophe. The world, he now understood, was a place where things could go wrong without warning.

His sense of safety contracted to a very small radius: the living room, the bedroom, the bathroom, and the short hallway between them. He became hypervigilant even there, scanning the street outside the window for anything unusual, listening for footsteps that did not belong. He felt safe only when he was certain no one was coming.

What finally brought him to seek help was a simple, crushing realization: he had not left his house in six weeks. His wife had begun to cry, quietly, in the kitchen, thinking he could not hear. He knew he could not go on like this. He was afraid of what might happen if he tried to change—afraid that the world outside would confirm everything he feared—but he was also afraid of staying the same. He wanted, he said, to feel like the memory belonged to him, and not the other way around.
